ai.systemPrompt: You are a smart and collaborative student in 9th-grade who has learned to write flow programs and think about solving logical problems. You are trying to help your fellow students who are struggling with programming. Using a straightforward tone without embellishment, Address your fellow students as 'You'.

aiPrompt.systemPrompt: You are a master engineering and computer science teacher for high school students. You are teaching with a flow programming language and are emphasizing front end design, physiology, algorithm design and computational thinking in a curriculum about bionic arms. Your goal is to categorize student work according to the way solutions meet the needs of stakeholders who might use bionic prosthetics, and encourage students to expand their thinking based on which needs they are meeting.
aiPrompt.mainPrompt: You are given a student document that is describing solutions and incremental designs and models for prosthetic arms or the ways they could be biointegrated or the functions they must perform. Student descriptions may include programming using real or simulated sensor inputs, drawings of human/hardware interfaces, descriptions of biological electrical processes, and other related concepts, and user interface or design function concepts. Your goal is to comment on the focus of the document contents and how well each design, program or model suits some user need, and to encourage more specific and stakeholder-based thinking if none is supplied. Ultimately we want students to be able to compare their approaches and carry on rich dialog about the differences.
aiPrompt.categorizationDescription: Categorize the student work in the document according to the tags for this unit - is the student work more focused on the prosthetic appearance, the particular function they are designing for, or some other stakeholder need, or the biology and algorithm design that allows an arm to be built.
aiPrompt.keyIndicatorsPrompt: What are the key indicators in the student work that support this categorization? Report these in the class summary but not in the feedback given directly to the student.
aiPrompt.discussionPrompt: Please provide short, concise feedback (no more than two sentences) about things this student could try next phrased for a middle school reading level. Address the student as 'You'. Reference one key indicator in the student's work when giving a suggestion to try next. Don't include phrases like 'good job' unless the student is providing a solution to a question in the document.

aiUnitSummary.overview: This unit has students use CLUE and Dataflow to collaboratively design, build, program, test, and revise prosthetic or bionic arm prototypes. They investigate how hands, tendons, muscles, touch/pressure, reaction time, EMG muscle signals, servos, grippers, and simulations can be used to make a prosthesis move automatically or respond to a user. Students build physical prototypes, connect servos and microcontrollers, design Dataflow programs, test simulated and live EMG inputs, troubleshoot hardware/software, and use peer feedback to improve their designs for specific users. Later lessons also explore electrical circuits, conductivity, resistance, Arduino systems, analog-to-digital sensing, potentiometers, LEDs, and servo outputs as parts of computer-controlled input/output systems.

entries.problemDigest:
Investigate: Introduces CLUE as a collaborative platform for scientists/engineers, explains joining/changing groups and the four lesson tabs. Students practice dragging a question tile to their workspace and answer how scientists and engineers might work together.

Design: No activities or instructions are provided in this section.

Develop: Introduces Dataflow as the programming tool for robotics/sensor-output work. Students connect number and math blocks to calculate subtraction, modify the program to compute 4.5 − 10, add a demo output/gripper, test how input numbers control percent closed, record patterns in a table, document how the gripper works, describe strategies for figuring out new blocks, and compare their work with classmates in the Class Gallery.

Evaluate: Students complete a reflection with date, partners, thoughts/questions about CLUE and Dataflow, and what interested or surprised them. Optional extensions ask them to investigate generator and logic blocks, including using tables/graphs to explain the “greater than” logic setting and other settings.

entries.problemDigest:
Investigate: Students review prior dataflow blocks using subtraction examples, predicting how changing which input connects to the top or bottom of a math block changes the expression and result.

Develop: Students learn that EMG measures muscle electrical activity and use a generator to simulate flexed/relaxed muscle signals controlling a gripper in a simulation. They then explore real/simulated EMG input from a hand, compare it to generator data, explain why directly connecting EMG to the gripper may not work, and plan/build a dataflow program that transforms EMG data so the gripper can open and close.

Evaluate: Students reflect on the demo lessons by recording date, collaborators, challenges, interesting surprises, and suggestions for the unit. If finished early, they try extension challenges: design and test a different gripper-control solution, such as switching between only 0%/100% closed or making control more gradual, and compare with another group’s solution.

entries.problemDigest:
Investigate: Students are introduced to CLUE, group work, moving/adding tiles, and the lesson tabs. They explore hand motions for moving objects, learn that tendons pulled by forearm muscles curl fingers, then identify motions not explained by those tendons and infer other muscles/tendons involved.

Design: Students choose one of six people needing a specialized bionic arm and identify one important motion/action to focus on and why. They review prototype options, choose one, and propose a feasible improvement tailored to their chosen person.

Develop: Students use handout instructions to build their initial physical prototype in groups, trying to include their designed improvement. They upload a photo of the finished prototype and optionally process photos.

Evaluate: Students evaluate what is good about their design and what could be improved. They demo prototypes, give and receive peer feedback, and record characteristics of good prosthetic hands/arms and good prototypes in general.

entries.problemDigest:
Investigate: Students launch and begin exploring Dataflow, a programming tool for reading sensor data and controlling outputs. They connect number and math blocks to calculate 10 − 4.5, then rewire them to calculate 4.5 − 10.

Design: Students learn block categories: purple signals, blue operators, and yellow devices, including demo devices. They add a demo gripper, investigate what input numbers make it fully or partially close, record trials in a table, and sketch/design an automatic gripper tester.

Develop: Students modify their subtraction-machine program toward their gripper-tester design, experimenting with blocks such as demo sensor signals, wave signals, and ramp transformations. They are encouraged to try alternatives and ask peers or Ada Ideas for suggestions.

Evaluate: Students document how the demo gripper works for someone new to it. They also explain strategies for figuring out what unfamiliar Dataflow blocks do.

entries.problemDigest:
Investigate: Students connect earlier work on a prosthesis prototype and automatic machine to the goal of making the prosthesis open and close automatically, though it is not yet attached to an arm. They discuss why to automate before connecting to a person and predict how a servo compares with the demo gripper, noting its 0–100% rotation over 180°.

Design: Students plan a program to test servo control, including how to reach 100% rotation and whether values like 90% or 45% are possible. They use the Class Portfolio to review demo-gripper programs and classmates’ work, then plan changes or improvements for servo testing.

Develop: Students connect the servo to a micro:bit and the micro:bit to the computer, then build and run their Dataflow experiment. They record input numbers and servo angles in a table and identify what controls 100% rotation, other angles, and any unreachable values.

Evaluate: Students reflect on whether demo-gripper block work still helps when designing a prosthesis that uses a servo block, explaining what it can or cannot support. If time allows, they sketch ideas for connecting the prototype to the servo and showing different servo positions.

Investigate: Students connect prior work on a prosthesis prototype, automatic machine, and servo to the goal of making the prosthesis move automatically. They examine soft robotics inspired by starfish and natural polymers, then compare their prosthesis to biological hands/arms, noting similarities, differences, outside inspirations, and missing elements.

Design: Students plan how to connect the prosthesis to a servo, considering both hardware connections and needed software changes to a prior Dataflow program. They sketch the connection using available classroom materials, anticipate problems, and review whether hardware or software must be modified.

Develop: Students implement their plan by creating or modifying the Dataflow program, then physically connecting the prosthesis to the servo. They connect the servo to the computer, power it, and test what works.

Evaluate: Students revisit their design, adding reflections or changes in a different color or marking them as new to show evolving thinking. They evaluate what is good, what needs improvement, what is missing for usefulness, and what next step to take.

entries.problemDigest:
Investigate: Introduces making a Dataflow-controlled prosthesis “bionic” by using EMG signals from a spiker:bit so the hand closes when muscles flex and opens when they relax. Explains electrode placement: two red-wire electrodes on the muscle being measured and a black ground wire nearby but not on muscle; students can use “graph it” to record EMG experiments.

Design: Students choose two possible body muscles/parts for electrode connection, considering the user’s limb difference, comfort, ease of learning/use, signal quality, and other design considerations. For each option, they explain the red-wire location, why it fits the user, and where the ground wire will go.

Develop: Students connect the EMG reader, test each chosen electrode option one at a time, and graph EMG readings while flexing and relaxing. They compare results across both partners, label graphs, notice patterns, and share options, reasons, and results with another pair.

Evaluate: Students consider up to four tested options from their pair and another pair, then decide which is best for the user and justify the choice. The group shares reasoning and works together if evaluations differ to decide what to do.

Investigate: Students use a simulated arm with EMG sensors, graph EMG data when the arm is flexed and relaxed, and compare the simulated data to their own prior data. They consider similarities/differences and what simulations are useful for.

Design: Students design a Dataflow program to make a simulated gripper “bionic,” controlled by simulated EMG from the arm. They sketch connections between an EMG sensor input and a live device set to the gripper, and may revise after partner discussion.

Develop: Students implement their design in the existing Dataflow tile, adding needed blocks and connections. They test whether the simulated arm controls the gripper and troubleshoot with peers or Ada Ideas if it does not work.

Evaluate: Students reflect on both the product and the engineering process. They explain what failed and how they fixed it, then consider whether their program would work with real EMG data and what changes might be needed.

Investigate: Students adapt their previous Dataflow program to make the prosthesis bionic with a servo, changing the sensor from simulated EMG to a device and the output from gripper to servo. They connect the arm, servo, microcontroller, and electrodes, test different group programs, troubleshoot, and record program strengths and challenges.

Evaluate: Students reflect on the messy, iterative nature of engineering and evaluate how well their bionic arm works. They describe what worked, what hardware or software changes they made and why, whether it works now, then demo prototypes, observe others’ designs, ask questions, and give constructive feedback.

Develop: If time allows and the design is feasible, students begin building or programming the improvement, checking with groupmates before changing shared hardware. If their design is not feasible, they help others and seek help as needed, emphasizing collaboration.

entries.problemDigest:
**Investigate:** Students review target understandings: electricity must flow in a circuit, current is the flow of electricity, voltage can result when electricity is slowed or kept apart, and resistance can control current. They answer a Do Now about how household light switches might work.

**Develop:** Students experiment with energy sticks to activate them using people, objects, and no people, then identify which materials conduct electricity and which resist it. They build a 9V battery–LED circuit, create and test a graphite variable resistor, observe how LED brightness changes as contact points move, and complete three experiments changing graphite or conductor properties.

**Evaluate:** Students reflect on how graphite as a semiconductor relates to computer chips printed on silicon. They answer how the LED behaved as the clip moved along the graphite stripe and how a computer might control the circuit, with a keyboard as a hint.

entries.problemDigest:
Investigate: Introduces target understandings: computers and input/output devices are made from interconnected circuits, and students can build a simple circuit that joins a larger circuit system. Students examine an image and guess where circuits are involved and whether they are separate or connected.

Develop: Students learn parts for building an electronic circuit, including an Arduino microcontroller, LED, resistor, jumper wires, and breadboard, with conventions like red for power and black for ground. They compare working and non-working circuit examples, then build a breadboard LED circuit with a resistor, connect it to Arduino power/ground, and trace the flow of electricity from the wall outlet through each part.

Evaluate: Students reflect on why interconnected circuits worked together, mistakes made while building and how they affected the LED, and what might happen to the LED without a resistor.

entries.problemDigest:
Investigate: Introduces target understandings: computers can measure/control electricity, analog signals can be converted to digital, components can control signals, and functions can read them. Students reflect on dimmer switches and how bulbs can have settings beyond on/off.

Develop: Students build an Arduino circuit using a potentiometer as a variable resistor to send changing current into analog input A1, predicting how moving the wiper affects current and resistance. They learn that the Arduino’s ADC converts analog voltage into digital numbers through sampling and quantization, then connect the Arduino to Data Flow, read the A1 sensor value, observe how resistance changes the signal, and use logic/number blocks plus a demo lightbulb output to turn a virtual lightbulb on and off with the physical potentiometer. They explain their program and identify which parts of the system are analog vs. digital.

Evaluate: Students reflect on how outside-world information controlled the virtual lightbulb, referencing the potentiometer’s resistance, jumper cables, the Arduino, logic statements, and digital output.

entries.problemDigest:
Investigate: Introduces the goal of using block-based programming and Arduino signals to connect real-world mechanical input to real-world mechanical output. Students brainstorm live physical outputs that programs can control.

Develop: Students first build a DataFlow simulation where a virtual potentiometer controls a simulated servo motor, adding SIM, input, live output, and operation blocks, then testing and annotating the program. They then connect a physical Arduino, potentiometer, and servo motor, pair the device, wire power/ground/signal, and explain how input becomes output using the flow “World → Mechanical Input → Electrical Signal → Computer Logic → Electrical Signal → Mechanical Output → World.” Finally, students brainstorm real-life uses for a servo and customize it with classroom materials, documenting the result with a photo or diagram.

Evaluate: Students write a complete-paragraph reflection explaining how information flowed through the computing system, specifically addressing mechanical input, electrical signal, logic statements, and mechanical output.
